activities.caption: fill the blanks — the four parts of every LP
activities.name: lpPartsCloze

config.text: Every LP is assembled from four parts: %%0%% variables (the quantities you may choose), an %%1%% function (a linear expression to maximise or minimise), %%2%% (linear inequalities capturing limited resources), and non-negativity.
config.hint: What you choose, what you score, what limits you.

activities.anchor: a well-posed LP is often worth as much as its solution
activities.caption: file each assumption as held or violated
activities.name: lpAssumeSort

config.prompt: The linearity contract — file each clause:

items.label: contributions scale with the variable — no setup costs or quantity discounts
effects of variables simply sum, with no interaction terms
fractional answers make sense — blending tonnes of ore
"build one more aircraft" — fractional output is nonsense
coefficients are known numbers, not gambles
a demand that arrives as a distribution — stochastic-programming territory

config.why: Proportionality, additivity, divisibility, certainty — knowing which world your variables live in is part of formulation, decided before any solver runs.

activities.caption: guess the magnitude — profit at the best corner
activities.name: lpVertexEstimate

config.prompt: The furniture workshop: 30 per table, 20 per chair, optimum at x1 = 10 tables, x2 = 20 chairs. What is the weekly profit there?
config.why: 30(10) + 20(20) = 700 — and every vertex scores: the origin 0, the single-binding corners 600 each, the intersection 700. Both resources fully used.
config.context: the four corners score 0, 600, 600, 700 — the corner wins

activities.anchor: bookkeeping that a computer performs at industrial scale
activities.caption: sequence the simplex walk
activities.name: lpSimplexOrder

config.prompt: The simplex method, step by step:
items: Start at any vertex of the feasible polygon
Look along the edges leaving it; pick the one that improves the objective fastest
Move along that edge to the next vertex — the profit rises
Stop when no leaving edge improves — the corner-point theorem guarantees that stopping rule is correct
config.why: Slack variables turn the inequalities into equations, and each pivot swaps one variable into the basis — a guided walk, not a search.

activities.anchor: the difference between checking a million corners and visiting a few dozen
activities.caption: bet before you read on — how many corners must simplex visit?
activities.name: lpWalkPredict

config.q: The corner-point theorem is proven. How many vertices must the simplex method actually visit in a two-thousand-variable LP?
choices: All of them — that is what guarantees optimality
A handful — each step's profit is strictly better, and it stops when no edge improves
Exactly one — the theorem names the optimal vertex directly
It depends on the solver brand
config.why: The theorem deletes the interior; the improving-walk rule deletes almost all the vertices. (Worst cases like the Klee–Minty cube exist, but practice is spectacular — and interior-point methods now share the load.)

activities.anchor: the free lunch the model refuses to serve
activities.caption: pair each duality term with its meaning
activities.name: lpDualMatch

config.prompt: Every plan has a price list — pair the terms:

pairs.right: the maximisation problem: choose the best plan
the minimisation problem built from the same data: price the resources
the profit added by one more unit of a binding resource
the best plan and the best price list meet exactly
a resource with slack prices at zero; a positive price must be produced

config.why: Discovered by von Neumann in 1947 (and embedded in Kantorovich's planning work, Nobel 1975) — duality is taught in economics departments as often as engineering ones.

activities.anchor: a third product whose profit would need to rise by 4 per unit before it earns a place in the mix
activities.caption: find the faulty line — the sensitivity brief
activities.name: lpSenseSpot

config.prompt: One line of this sensitivity brief is wrong — click it:
lines: The shadow price says what a resource is worth at the margin: overtime below 10 per hour raises profit.
Airlines run the same logic on gates and landing slots; refineries on crude qualities.
Reduced costs price the products already in the plan — confirming what you already make.
Ranging asks how far a coefficient can move before the current basis stops being optimal.
Complementary slackness ties it together: slack means zero price.
config.correction: Reduced costs price the variables left OUT of the plan — what a missing product must earn before it enters the mix.
config.why: Sensitivity analysis separates the priced-in from the priced-out, and ranging defines how far every price stays valid.
